client: I've been really struggling since last week's team meeting at work. My colleague called out some mistakes I made in front of everyone, and I can't stop replaying it in my head — it just keeps making me feel like I'm completely incompetent. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like that moment really stung, and having it happen in front of others makes it especially hard to shake — that kind of public embarrassment has a way of looping in our minds and feeling much bigger than it might actually be. I'm really glad you decided to give this a try, even with some doubt about whether it'll help, because that kind of honest skepticism is actually a great starting point for us to work with. When that memory replays, what's the specific thought that tends to hit you the hardest — is it something like "I always mess up," or does it take a different shape for you?

client: The thought that keeps coming back is more like "everyone in that room now thinks I'm incompetent, and nothing I do going forward will change that impression." It's less about always messing up in general and more about feeling permanently defined by that one moment in front of those specific people. And the worst part is I have to see them every day, so it's not like I can just move on and forget it happened.
therapist: That thought — feeling permanently defined by one moment in the eyes of people you see every day — sounds really heavy to carry, like there's no escape from it. One thing worth gently examining is whether that thought is a fact or a conclusion your mind jumped to: do you have actual evidence that your colleagues have permanently written you off, or might your mind be filling in the gaps with the worst possible interpretation? What do you think those colleagues actually saw — just a mistake, or something that truly defines your entire value to them?

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically I know I don't have hard proof that they've written me off permanently. But it doesn't feel like my mind is just filling in gaps — it feels like I'm reading the room accurately, because ever since that meeting a couple of people have been quieter around me than usual. That silence feels like confirmation, even if I can't be a hundred percent sure that's what it means.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can hold both things at once — knowing logically there's no hard proof, while still feeling like the silence is telling you something real. In CBT we call this "emotional reasoning," where the feeling itself becomes the evidence, but it's worth asking: could there be other explanations for your colleagues being quieter — like their own stress, distractions, or just normal fluctuation in how people interact week to week? If a close friend described this exact situation to you, what alternative explanations might you offer them before concluding their colleagues had permanently judged them?

client: I guess if a friend told me this, I'd probably say "maybe they're just busy" or "people have their own stuff going on." But it's so much harder to apply that same logic to myself — when it's happening to me, those alternative explanations just feel like excuses I'm making to avoid the obvious. I think part of what makes this so hard is that I already had some underlying doubts about whether I really belong on this team, so this incident just kind of confirmed what I was already afraid of.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really important — the incident didn't create this fear, it landed on top of doubts that were already there, which is why it feels so much more like "confirmation" than just a rough moment. That pre-existing sense of not belonging is worth exploring, because it's likely the lens through which you're interpreting everything, including your colleagues' silence. Where do you think those doubts about belonging on this team originally came from — were they there from the very start, or did something specific plant that seed?

client: Honestly, I think those doubts were there from day one — this team has a lot of people with more experience than me, and I've always felt like I snuck in somehow, like they made a mistake hiring me. There was also a comment my manager made about three months in about me "still having a learning curve," which at the time I brushed off but looking back it kind of lodged itself in my head. So I've basically been waiting for the moment when everyone else would see what I already suspected about myself.
therapist: What you're describing has a name — it's often called "impostor syndrome," and it's incredibly common among people who are actually quite capable, which tells us something important: this feeling of having "snuck in" is more about a story you've been carrying than an accurate reflection of your abilities. That one comment from your manager about a learning curve — which is honestly pretty normal feedback for someone newer to a role — got stored as evidence for a fear that was already looking for proof. I'm curious: when you think back over your time on this team, are there moments or pieces of work that *don't* fit the story that you don't belong — things you've quietly pushed aside because they didn't match the narrative?

client: There are a few things, yeah — I led a project last quarter that got positive feedback, and my manager actually thanked me specifically in an email for catching an error that would have cost the team a lot of time. But when you ask me to hold onto those as evidence that I belong, it feels almost dishonest, like I'm cherry-picking the good stuff to feel better while ignoring the real picture. I think that's what worries me about this whole reframing approach — it feels like I'm just trying to talk myself into feeling okay rather than actually dealing with whether my fears have any truth to them.
therapist: Your concern about reframing is actually a really thoughtful one, and it shows a lot of intellectual honesty — but here's something worth sitting with: you're applying completely different standards to each type of evidence. The mistakes feel like "the real picture," while the project success and your manager's specific praise get labeled as cherry-picking — but why should the negative automatically count as more truthful than the positive? What if the most accurate picture isn't the worst one or the best one, but one that holds both, and you've just been trained by that underlying fear to treat the negative as the default truth?

client: That actually lands a little differently than I expected — the idea that I'm holding the negative and positive evidence to different standards. I hadn't thought about it that way, but I think you're right that I automatically assume the bad stuff is more "real" or more telling about who I actually am. I'm still not sure I can just decide to trust the positive evidence the same way, though — it feels like that would take a lot of practice and I honestly don't know if I'm capable of shifting something that feels this deeply wired into how I see myself.
therapist: It's really encouraging that that idea landed for you, and I want to gently push back on one thing: you just described a deeply ingrained pattern of thinking with clarity and insight that many people never reach, which is itself evidence that you *are* capable of shifting this — it just won't happen all at once, and it doesn't need to. You're not being asked to suddenly trust the positive evidence completely, but rather to slowly practice giving it the same *right to exist* as the negative, like a muscle you build gradually rather than a switch you flip. What do you think it would feel like to treat that manager's email — just that one piece of evidence — as equally real and valid as the memory of last week's meeting?

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine holding that email as equally real as last week's meeting, there's a small part of me that feels something like... relief, almost, like I'd be putting down something heavy for a second. But then almost immediately there's this voice that says "yeah but the email was months ago and the meeting was last week, so the meeting is more current and therefore more true." I don't know how to argue with that voice when it feels so logical in the moment.
therapist: That moment of relief you noticed is really significant — your mind and body are giving you a glimpse of what it might feel like to carry this differently, and that's worth holding onto. As for that voice telling you the meeting is "more current and therefore more true" — that's a clever argument, but it's worth questioning the logic: does something being recent automatically make it more defining than a pattern of success built over months? If we only ever judged ourselves by the most recent difficult moment, none of us would ever feel secure — so what would it mean to let *recency* be just one data point rather than the deciding vote?

client: That reframe about recency actually makes some sense to me — like, I wouldn't tell a friend that one bad week erases months of solid work, so why does my brain treat it that way for me. But I think what scares me is that even if I intellectually accept that recency shouldn't be the deciding vote, I still have to walk into that office tomorrow and face those people, and the anxiety in my body doesn't really care about logical arguments in the moment. How do I actually use any of this when I'm standing there in real time and the fear just takes over?
therapist: You're hitting on something really important — there's a gap between understanding something intellectually and having it available to you when your nervous system is activated, and that gap is completely normal and real. One practical CBT tool for exactly this moment is to prepare a short "grounding phrase" in advance — something like "one moment doesn't define months of work" — that you've already connected to emotionally, so it's ready to interrupt the spiral before it takes over rather than trying to construct the argument from scratch while anxious. When you imagine walking in tomorrow, is there one specific moment you're most dreading — like a particular interaction or just the general weight of entering the room — that we could think through together so you feel a little more prepared?

client: The moment I'm dreading most is probably running into my colleague — the one who called out my mistakes — in the kitchen or hallway, somewhere without the structure of a meeting where I'd have to just make normal small talk and pretend everything's fine. I like the idea of a grounding phrase in theory, but I worry that in that specific moment my mind will just go blank and the phrase will feel hollow or rehearsed rather than actually calming. Is there something more concrete I can do with my body or my attention in that moment, because I feel like my thoughts are too unreliable to be the anchor?
therapist: Your instinct to anchor in your body rather than your thoughts in that moment is actually really wise — when anxiety spikes, the body is often more accessible than the mind. A simple technique is the "5-4-3-2-1" grounding method: briefly and discreetly notice 5 things you can see, 4 you can feel physically (like your feet on the floor or hands around a mug), and it naturally pulls your attention out of the fear spiral and back into the present moment before the conversation even begins. And here's something worth considering about that interaction itself: you don't have to "pretend everything's fine" perfectly — just getting through a 30-second exchange about coffee is enough of a win, so what would it look like to set that as your only goal for that moment rather than managing how you feel the whole time?
